newsitem.title: USA: One year later, Simpson verdict still questioned.
newsitem.headline: One year later, Simpson verdict still questioned.

text.p: One year to the day after O.J. Simpson was acquitted of double murder charges, prospective jurors in his civil trial on Thursday voiced sharply divided opinions over his guilt or innocence.

A black man who appeared to be in his 30s told attorneys that he agreed with the verdicts in the criminal trial because police investigators "bungled" the evidence, while a Hispanic man in his 30s said he considered Simpson a guilty man who used "money and 10 good attorneys" to win his freedom.
Both men were excused by Judge Hiroshi Fujisaki as too biased for a case in which race played such a key role.

Last Oct. 3, Simpson, a former football star who is black, was found not guilty of the June 12, 1994, stabbing murders of his ex-wife, Nicole Brown Simpson, and her friend Ronald Goldman, both of whom were white.
He is currently battling a wrongful-death lawsuit filed by the families of the murder victims.

In a moment of levity during Thursday's otherwise mundane jury selection process, laughter rang out in the courtroom as the opinion of one prospective juror as stated in a questionnaire was read to the court.

"I think the dude's an idiot," the man wrote of Simpson's flight from justice during a slow-speed chase on the day he was to have surrendered to authorities. "You just can't ride until you get to the border," the man, a Latino in his 20s, added in the questionnaire.

As jury selection continued in the Santa Monica courthouse, officials from the National Association for the Advancement of Coloured People gathered outside to protest the lenient sentence given to a key figure in the criminal trial.

On Wednesday, ex-detective Mark Fuhrman, who was alleged by Simpson's defence to have planted a bloody glove on Simpson's estate, was sentenced to three years' probation after pleading no contest to a perjury charge.
His plea, the equivalent of a guilty plea under California law, was an admission that he lied on the stand when he said he had not called black people "niggers" in the past 10 years.
"Mark Fuhrman should have gone to jail like any other person and the fact that he is going to Idaho (where he now lives) ... sends the wrong message to black people," said a NAACP official.

Another NAACP leader, Geraldine Washington, said the plea- bargain agreement of three years' probation and a $200 fine was "a mockery of justice. This creates grave chagrin for people of colour," she said.
Another 10 jurors -- three blacks, four Latinos and three whites -- were added on Thursday to the pool which will face further questioning next week.
So far, 80 people have been chosen for the next round of jury selection. Fujisaki reportedly wants a pool of about 100 potential jurors before starting that process.
